shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner descending on a standard arrival route towards an airport. Visual conditions, at dawn.

The crew. The first officer was the pilot flying and the captain the pilot monitoring. The captain had about 17,400 hours, 4,000 on type.

What happened. At 15,000 ft, ATC cleared the aircraft to cross a fix at 10,000 ft and then to fly at 250 knots. The first officer began trying to meet the crossing altitude while slowing to 250 knots. The captain reset the selected speed to 300 knots, explaining that the higher speed would help the descent and that 250 knots was not needed until after the 10,000 ft crossing. As the aircraft was high, the captain asked ATC for relief from the 10,000 ft crossing, and ATC granted it. The first officer had selected vertical speed mode at 5,000 ft per minute down. The speed quickly increased past 300 knots, even with the speed brakes extended. As the speed trend arrow approached the overspeed limit and the speed approached 320 knots, the first officer disconnected the autopilot and pitched up to stop the speed increasing. The captain saw the g-load indication appear and told the first officer to make smaller control inputs. The captain then saw the g-load read 1.4 g and then 1.6 g. Looking back at the flight display, the captain saw the pitch attitude at 10 degrees nose up. The pitch was corrected almost at once, and the g-load indication went out.
safe_outcome: The aircraft continued down to 10,000 ft at a normal rate of descent and then slowed to 250 knots. The rest of the flight was normal. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was descending nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
notes: Removed under rule 3: nothing in the narrative is later reflection; NASA's synopsis wording ('caused an overspeed and temporary loss of control') is not used. Kept: the captain's reasons at the time for resetting the speed and for asking for relief; the first officer's reason for pitching up (to stop the speed increase), as the captain reported it. Moved under rule 5: the continued descent to 10,000 ft, slowing to 250 knots and the rest of the flight. Removed under rule 6: arrival, fix and airport names. Cut for length: the captain's 210 hours in the previous 90 days. Judgement calls: the report does not say what replaced the 10,000 ft crossing once relief was granted, so nothing is added. The report's 'G meter' is written as the g-load indication. Bracket 'descending': the aircraft was descending on an arrival, where other arrival traffic is also descending; 'crossing' would also fit the abrupt pitch-up.
